INTRODUCTION

Autonomous robotics demands real time adaptive behaviour under noisy, dynamic physical environments ; a challenge that rigid hand coded controllers fail to meet
Biological organisms solve this through tightly coupled neural, chemical, and bodily feedback loops operating across multiple temporal and spatial scales
Cognitive Autonomous Recurrent Lifeform (CARL) is proposed as a biologically inspired digital organism, simulated within the MuJoCo physics engine, to replicate these multi scale biological control principles
CARL is a biologically inspired digital organism architecture designed to progressively integrate seven biological and computational mechanisms through staged development: an LSM reservoir brain, 4 factor endocrine neuromodulation (Dopamine, Serotonin, Norepinephrine, Acetylcholine), Spike Timing Dependent Plasticity (STDP), hippocampal grid/place cell navigation, a Free Energy active inference engine, Physarum style adaptive route reinforcement, and a mirror neuron based social learning layer
Traditional autonomous systems treat perception, navigation, memory, and motor control as isolated software modules ; leading to brittle integration and failure under environmental perturbation
Biological brains maintain robustness through continuous prediction error minimisation (Free Energy Principle), neuromodulatory gain control, and activity dependent synaptic reorganisation

texts: LITERATURE SUMMARY

High fidelity simulation, contact dynamics, friction and scalable digital twin environments are essential for testing embodied robotic behaviour before physical deployment
Reservoir and liquid time constant architectures show that recurrent systems can represent evolving sensorimotor dynamics while maintaining computational efficiency
Spiking networks and STDP demonstrate that temporal neural representations can support fast, event driven motor control and adaptation to changing dynamics
Biological neuromodulators indicate that learning and behaviour are not governed by a fixed gain; internal state can regulate attention, plasticity, exploration and behavioural response
Grid cell, place cell and head direction mechanisms provide a biologically grounded framework for path integration, spatial representation and correction of accumulated navigation error
Physarum inspired approaches show that network reinforcement can produce efficient, adaptive routes under changing or uncertain conditions
Model Predictive Path Integral control (MPPI) and related sampling based methods demonstrate that future action trajectories can be evaluated online rather than relying only on instantaneous reactive control
Active inference frameworks provide a common perspective linking perception, prediction, action and uncertainty driven behaviour
The literature supports the feasibility of combining these mechanisms into a staged biologically inspired robotic architecture; however, existing studies generally investigate these mechanisms independently rather than as one progressively validated embodied cognitive system
RESEARCH GAP

No single reviewed architecture combines a liquid/reservoir temporal controller with a risk aware, sampling based trajectory optimizer inside one real time embodied control loop
Limited work couples multi factor endocrine neuromodulation (DA/NE/5 HT/ACh) with liquid time constant or reservoir based brains for continuous autonomous control
No reviewed work directly couples hippocampal continuous attractor grid cells with a real time MuJoCo physics based motor controller under Physarum style adaptive route reinforcement
Reviewed active inference frameworks operate independently from endocrine neuromodulation and Physarum style route reinforcement; no architecture unifies all three within one digital twin control loop
OBJECTIVE

To develop and progressively validate CARL, a physics grounded biologically inspired cognitive robotic architecture integrating sensorimotor, temporal, spatial, predictive and adaptive behavioural mechanisms within a real time digital twin environment
PROBLEM STATEMENT

Existing robotic systems commonly employ independently designed perception, navigation, prediction, and control modules, limiting adaptive behaviour under changing physical conditions. The fragmented integration of embodied sensorimotor dynamics, temporal and spatial cognition, predictive modelling, and prospective action selection remains a challenge within unified real-time physics-based environments.
